exercise.title: What is the difference between a sequence and a series?

statement.p: A sequence asks whether the terms settle. A series asks whether the accumulated partial sums settle. In your own words, why is that a different question even when both objects are built from the same list a_k?

hint.p: The terms can become small while the running totals keep climbing. The series is not the list; it is the limit of finite sums of the list.

exercise.title: Why do positive series and signed series ask different questions?

statement.p: A positive series converges exactly when its increasing partial sums are bounded. An alternating series can converge by organized cancellation. In your own words, why does the presence or absence of cancellation change the whole strategy?

hint.p: With no cancellation, the only issue is a ceiling. With signs, the issue is whether corrections shrink in a controlled way, or whether the total size is finite without needing them.

note.title: Computing lesson
note.p: A long list of partial sums can suggest a pattern, but it cannot replace a theorem. Slow divergence can look like convergence for a very long time.

exercise.title: Why does the kind of convergence decide whether rearrangement is safe?

statement.p: Absolutely convergent series keep the same sum under rearrangement. Conditionally convergent series need not. In your own words, why is finite total size the difference between a robust infinite sum and a fragile cancellation pattern?

hint.p: Absolute convergence means the total magnitude of all terms is finite, so a sufficiently late tail is small regardless of order. Conditional convergence has infinite positive and negative totals, so order can steer their balance.

exercise.title: What new question appears when series terms contain a variable?

statement.p: The next chapter turns numerical series into expressions such as 1+x+x^2+\cdots. In your own words, why does an infinite sum with a variable become a candidate for a function, and what extra question must be asked that a numerical series never faced?

hint.p: For each input, the expression is a numerical series that may converge or diverge. The new question is the domain: for which x does the infinite polynomial make sense?
